## 1.

I collect a data set with $n = 100$ observations containing a single
predictor and a quantitative response. I fit a linear regression
$Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X + \varepsilon$, as well as a separate cubic
regression $Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X + \beta_2 X^2 + \beta_3 X^3 + \varepsilon$.

a. Suppose the true relationship between $X$ and $Y$ is linear. Compare the training RSS of the linear and cubic fits. Is one lower, are they the same, or is there not enough information to tell? Justify your answer.
b. Answer part a using test RSS rather than training RSS.
c. Suppose the true relationship between $X$ and $Y$ is not linear, but we do not know how far it is from linear. Answer part a in this setting.
d. Answer part c using test RSS rather than training RSS.

## 2.

Consider simple linear regression without an intercept, so the $i$th fitted
value is $\hat{y}_i = x_i\hat\beta$, where

$$\hat\beta = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i}{\sum_{j=1}^n x_j^2}.$$

a. Show that $\hat{y}_i$ can be written as $\sum_{j=1}^n a_j y_j$. What is $a_j$?
b. This says the fitted values are linear combinations of the responses. In the matrix form from lecture, $\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{H}\mathbf{y}$. Which entry of $\mathbf{H}$ is $a_j$ for observation $i$, and what does the diagonal entry $h_i$ measure?
c. Now return to a model with an intercept. Using the normal equations $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\hat\beta = \mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y}$, argue that the residuals sum to zero, and use this to show that the least squares line in simple linear regression always passes through the point $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$.
